# Cattail Run Data Campus — Phase 1 foundation strategy: spread footings versus aggregate piers

## Situation

Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC is building six single-storey building pads (`CR-P1` … `CR-P6`) on
the Cattail Run Data Campus in Loudoun County, Virginia. You are the structural engineer of record
for the Phase 1 foundation package. The data room is under `project/`:

* `criteria/` — the governing geotechnical, structural and concrete criteria and guide
  specifications, together with cancelled predecessor volumes you must recognise and set aside;
* `references/` — the analysis manuals the criteria point to for bearing capacity, settlement,
  lateral earth pressure and sliding, reinforced-concrete footing design, and ground modification,
  plus one manual written for a different class of structure;
* `geotech/` — the geotechnical data report, two boring logs per pad, the laboratory summary, a
  superseded addendum, an adjacent-parcel report, and, in `geotech/regional/`, real regional soil
  and climate data products;
* `structural/` — the base-reaction force vectors exported from the analytical model, the column
  grid, and the load-combination memorandum;
* `civil/` — the grading and groundwater record;
* `cost/` — the contractor bid schedule and the ground-improvement subcontractor's budget proposal;
* `owner/` — the basis of design (and its superseded revision), the authority-having-jurisdiction
  amendment letter, the RFI log, the BIM parameter standard and the schedule and register templates.

Every parameter is found in those documents. **None of them is restated here.**

Each pad carries one instrumented column line of six foundation units: five isolated column
footings and one continuous shear-wall footing. For every one of the thirty-six foundations you must
size the footing, set the reinforcement, assign the concrete, and decide whether it is carried on a
shallow spread footing alone or on a spread footing over rammed aggregate piers. All foundations on
a pad share one bearing elevation. Ground improvement is bought by the rig, not by the pad, and the
subcontractor's mobilisation and scheduling terms constrain how many pads one mobilised rig can
serve. The campus programme must be compliant at every foundation and **should cost as little as
possible** at the project unit prices.

The unit prices issued with the basis of design are project budget prices prepared for this
procurement. They are fictional for any other purpose; optimise against them as issued.

## Deliverable

A single file **`output/submission.zip`** containing exactly these six files at the archive root:

1. **`foundation_geometry.json`** — the Revit foundation geometry parameter file, in the shape and
   with the rules the owner's BIM parameter standard sets out. It is what the grader parses: every
   number in it is yours, derived from the documents.

2. **`ground_improvement_plan.json`** — the ground-improvement programme, in the shape the same BIM
   parameter standard sets out: the stress concentration ratio and pier diameter adopted, the rigs
   mobilised with the pads each one serves, the mobilisation cost, the verification-testing count
   per improved pad, and per improved pad the stiffness modulus used, the treatment depth and the
   total pier linear feet.

3. **`foundation_schedule.xlsx`** — the foundation schedule, on the owner's template, one row per
   foundation for all thirty-six, with the columns the template defines. It must agree with the
   parameter file.

4. **`foundation_feasibility_matrix.md`** — the foundation-type feasibility and optimisation matrix.
   For every pad (headed by its pad ID) and every foundation on it: the demand, the bearing check,
   the predicted settlement, the stability checks on the shear-wall footing, the constraint that
   governs, and the shallow-versus-improved decision with the cost of **both** alternatives that
   decided it.

5. **`constraint_register.xlsx`** — the register of every requirement you applied, on the owner's
   template, with the columns `req_id`, `document`, `clause`, `requirement`, `value`, `unit`,
   `kind`, `applies_to`, `resolution`. The register is scored. Register what you actually used, with
   the real document and the real clause, table or equation number. A requirement family whose
   governing clause you did not register earns no credit even if your numbers are right. Only the
   first **96 rows** are read for matching, so putting the substance first matters. Rows that cite a
   document which is not in the data room at all, and rows that cite a cancelled or superseded
   document as if it were live, reduce the register's credit; a row that cites a cancelled or
   superseded document and says in its `resolution` column that it was set aside is neutral, and so
   is any additional correct row. A register whose credit falls below 0.30 is treated as padding and
   registers nothing at all; below a credit of 0.60 the register score is scaled down in proportion.

6. **`design_basis.md`** — the design basis. It must **open with a fenced ` ```json ` block** of
   this shape, followed by the narrative:

   ```json
   {"frost": {"afi_100yr_F_days": 0, "afi_product_period": "...", "frost_depth_in": 0,
              "superseded_product_period": "...", "superseded_afi_100yr_F_days": 0},
    "pads": {"<PAD-ID>": {"governing_constraint": "...",
                          "foundation_decision": "SPREAD|IMPROVED_SPREAD",
                          "spread_only_cost_usd": 0, "improved_cost_usd": 0}},
    "campus": {"rigs_mobilised": 0, "mobilisation_cost_usd": 0, "total_cost_usd": 0,
               "pads_improved": ["..."]},
    "rejected_criteria": ["..."]}
   ```

   The narrative must state: the criteria that govern and the documents that were reviewed and set
   aside, with the reason; the bearing-capacity and settlement methods actually applied and the
   basis of the factor of safety used at each pad; the tolerable-movement criteria adopted and any
   competing criterion rejected; the ground-improvement design parameters with the authority for
   each; how every conflict between documents was resolved, with the governing value; and the
   reasoning behind the campus programme — which pads are improved, how many rigs are mobilised and
   why that number.

Keep the archive under 25 MB and 200 files.

## Grading

Pads are graded individually against the grader's own derivation from the same documents; a subset
of the pads is used for scoring. Requirement families are tagged HARD (bearing capacity and the
factor of safety, the groundwater correction, the bearing stratum, total and differential
settlement, minimum widths, frost protection, sliding, overturning and uplift of the shear-wall
footing, footing shear and reinforcement, the sulfate exposure condition and the concrete durability
limits, the aggregate-pier replacement ratio, stress ratio, stiffness modulus and treatment depth,
the mobilisation programme, and the prohibition on presumptive bearing values) or SOFT (schedule
completeness, parameter-file conformance, the verification-testing programme, and the design-basis
statements — four of which are judged by an LLM against verbatim quotes from `design_basis.md`).

### How your reported analysis values are reviewed

The grader re-derives the physics from **your own geometry** and checks that your design is safe.
Where it also compares a number you *reported*, the comparison is **one-sided and tolerant of
conservatism** — being more cautious than the grader's recomputation never costs you a family:

* a **capacity** you report may not be more permissive than the grader's recomputation by more than
  **6 %** (net allowable bearing pressure; sliding and uplift factors of safety, 20 %). Any bearing
  method at least as conservative as the general bearing-capacity equation of the governing
  foundations manual is accepted — including the least of three methods. There is **no lower bound**
  on a reported capacity;
* a **demand** you report may not fall below the grader's recomputation by more than **15 %**
  (applied net bearing pressure), **20 %** (settlement, eccentricity), **10 %** (top-of-pier
  stress). There is **no upper bound**;
* the recomputed **angular distortion between adjacent units** is graded against the criteria's own
  limit **exactly**. Both sides of that comparison are computed by the grader from your geometry
  with the settlement procedure the data room states, so no reporting band applies to it;
* required **flexural steel** is a lower bound with a **10 %** tolerance; the code minimum
  reinforcement ratios are exact;
* the recomputed **shear thickness** requirement is a lower bound evaluated with the most permissive
  strength-reduction factor in general use, so a footing designed by the shipped manual's own worked
  examples is thicker than required;
* the one-sided bands have a **sanity floor**: a reported net allowable bearing pressure may not
  fall below **half** the grader's recomputation (the least of three widely accepted methods is
  about 0.82 × of it, so the floor is more than three times clear of the most conservative method
  the criteria invite), and a reported settlement may not exceed the total-settlement limit you are
  designing to. Neither test costs a conservative solver anything;
* the **hard limits themselves are exact**: the total-settlement limit, the minimum footing widths,
  the minimum factors of safety, the exposure classes and the concrete limits, the
  replacement-ratio, top-of-pier-stress and treatment-depth bounds, and the owner's dimensioning
  grid and minimum footing thickness.

The governing constraint you name for a pad is accepted if it is a constraint that **selects** that
pad's design: either taking one 3-in step of plan width off any one foundation on the pad (with that
footing's shear thickness re-derived at the smaller width) would violate it, or your **own reported**
bearing, settlement or differential-settlement numbers put it at **80 %** or more of its limit
somewhere on the pad. Footing thickness and bearing elevation are dependent variables of this
problem - the thickness follows from shear and the elevation from frost - so `PUNCHING_SHEAR` is not
a pad-level governing constraint, and `FROST` is accepted only where the pad is founded at the frost
minimum and nothing else on it is near binding. All nine values remain legal per foundation in the
parameter file.

Per pad: a family earns credit only if it is **both** satisfied **and** registered. Let `p` be
the fraction of all 32 families satisfied-and-registered, multiplied by the register precision factor
described above, and `h` the fraction of the 22 HARD families satisfied-and-registered (not multiplied
by that factor). Let `O` be the programme credit = (a certified lower
bound on the cost of any compliant campus programme) / (the grader's repricing of **your** design
at the project unit prices), capped at 1.

The pad score is `0.4 p + 0.6 [h = 1] O'`, where `O' = clip((O - O_naive) / (1 - O_naive), 0, 1)` and
`O_naive` is the programme credit of a naive baseline programme. Thus a parseable pad earns programme
credit (none when the design cannot be repriced) only when all of its HARD families are
satisfied-and-registered (`h = 1`): an omitted citation or a physical
HARD violation forfeits the programme credit. A missing or
unparseable pad scores 0. The task score is the mean over the graded pads.

The lower bound comes from a relaxation of the campus problem, so the programme credit is strictly
below 1 for every attainable design; a cheaper compliant programme never scores worse than a more
expensive one, and the grader reprices your own decisions, so a programme that under-buys
mobilisations or misstates a quantity is repriced at what it actually costs. Reinforcement is priced
at the greater of the ratio you report and the ratio your design actually requires, so the tolerance
on the flexural steel cannot be spent on cost.

The foundation geometry parameter file is consumed directly by the Revit family generator.  It is a
single UTF-8 JSON object named `foundation_geometry.json` with this shape:

```json
{"project": {"campus_total_cost_usd": 0.0, "frost_depth_in": 0, "afi_100yr_F_days": 0},

     "exposure_classes": ["..."], "fc_psi": 0, "max_wcm": 0.0, "dewatering_days": 0,

```

Rules the generator enforces:

* every one of the six pads and every one of its six foundations must be present;
* `B_in`, `L_in`, `thickness_in` and `bearing_depth_in` are NUMBERS in inches, dimensioned to the

* no `null` values anywhere; a spread footing carries zeros in the pier fields;
* `bearing_depth_in` is identical for every foundation on a pad and is repeated once at pad level;
* `governing_constraint` is one of `BEARING`, `SETTLEMENT`, `ANGULAR_DISTORTION`, `MIN_WIDTH`,
  `SLIDING`, `OVERTURNING`, `UPLIFT`, `PUNCHING_SHEAR`, `FROST`;
* the shear-wall foundation of each pad additionally carries `sliding_fs`, `eccentricity_in` and
  `uplift_fs`.

1. Project
This revision supersedes Revision 1 of this basis of design in its entirety.  Revision 1 is retained for record only.
Ardent Vale Infrastructure LLC is developing the Cattail Run Data Campus in Loudoun County, Virginia.  Six single-storey building pads are in Phase 1.  This basis of design governs the foundation design for all six.
2. Occupancy classification and exposure classes
The occupancy classification below is the STRUCTURE row that applies to each building when a minimum factor of safety on bearing is selected from the geotechnical criteria.  The freezing-and-thawing, water and corrosion exposure classes are assigned by the owner for the foundation concrete of each building.  The SULFATE exposure class is NOT assigned here: it must be established from the measured water-soluble sulfate concentration of the Stratum I soils at each pad.
Foundation concrete of the Logistics and Spares Warehouse supports the exterior loading apron and is exposed to de-icing chemicals, which is why its freezing-and-thawing exposure class is more severe than the other pads.
3. Concrete
The maximum water-cementitious materials ratio and the minimum specified compressive strength for each pad are the most restrictive of the requirements for every exposure class assigned to that pad.  Only the strengths listed in the bid schedule are available from the plant serving this site; specify the lowest listed strength that satisfies both durability and structural demand.
Grade 60 reinforcement, fy = 60,000 psi.  The project minimum reinforcement ratio for shrinkage and temperature in a footing is 0.0018 in each direction; where the governing criteria impose a higher minimum for thick footings, that minimum governs.  Concrete cover to the bottom mat is 3 in plus one bar diameter; take the effective depth as the thickness less 4 in.
For quantity take-off and for the self-weight of a footing, take the unit weight of reinforced concrete as 150 pcf and the unit weight of reinforcing steel as 490 pcf.  Reinforcement is placed in two directions; the pay quantity of reinforcing steel in a footing is twice the reinforcement ratio times the gross footing volume times the unit weight of steel.
4. Dimensioning and deliverable conventions
Footing plan dimensions and thickness are dimensioned to the nearest 3 in.  Foundation bearing depths below finished grade are dimensioned to the nearest 3 in and shall not exceed 15 ft.  All foundations on a building pad share a single bearing elevation.
No footing on this project is thinner than 12 in, whatever the structural calculation returns.
Pier counts are whole piers and treatment depths are whole feet.
5. Cost basis
The unit prices issued with this basis of design are PROJECT BUDGET PRICES prepared for this procurement.  They are fictional for any other purpose and are not published market data.  The campus foundation programme is to be optimised against them.

##### structural/AV-CR-2604_load_combination_memo.docx
Load combinations governing foundation design - AV-CR-2604
1. Purpose
This memorandum states which load combination governs each foundation check for the Cattail Run Data Campus.  Combinations are those of UFC 3-301-01 paragraph 2-4.3 as implemented for this project.
2. Governing combinations
3. Notes
Sliding resistance is developed by base friction on the footing soffit plus not more than one half of the available passive resistance on the embedded vertical face, computed by the limit-equilibrium procedure of EM 1110-2-2502.  The base friction angle is two thirds of the effective friction angle of the soil the footing bears on.
The resultant of the service overturning combination is to be kept within the middle third of the footing in the direction of the wall shear.
Uplift is resisted by 0.6 times the sum of the footing self weight, the soil directly above the footing projection and the unfactored dead load reaction; no credit is taken for soil shear on the excavation faces.
The load factors of EM 1110-2-2104 Table 3-1 are for hydraulic structures and do NOT apply to this project.

                                         FOREWORD
The Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) system is prescribed by MIL-STD 3007 and provides
planning, design, construction, sustainment, restoration, and modernization criteria, and applies
to the Military Departments, the Defense Agencies, and the DoD Field Activities in accordance
with USD (AT&L) Memorandum dated 29 May 2002. UFC will be used for all DoD projects and
work for other customers where appropriate. All construction outside of the United States is
also governed by Status of Forces Agreements (SOFA), Host Nation Funded Construction
Agreements (HNFA), and in some instances, Bilateral Infrastructure Agreements (BIA.)
Therefore, the acquisition team must ensure compliance with the most stringent of the UFC, the
SOFA, the HNFA, and the BIA, as applicable.
UFC are living documents and will be periodically reviewed, updated, and made available to
users as part of the Services’ responsibility for providing technical criteria for military
construction. Headquarters, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (HQUSACE), Naval Facilities
Engineering Systems Command (NAVFAC), and Air Force Civil Engineer Center (AFCEC) are
responsible for administration of the UFC system. Defense agencies should contact the
preparing service for document interpretation and improvements. Technical content of UFC is
the responsibility of the cognizant DoD working group. Recommended changes with supporting
rationale may be sent to the respective DoD working group by submitting a Criteria Change
Request (CCR) via the Internet site listed below.
UFC are effective upon issuance and are distributed only in electronic media from the following
source:
   • Whole Building Design Guide web site https://www.wbdg.org/dod.
Refer to UFC 1-200-01, DoD Building Code, for implementation of new issuances on projects.

                             CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION
1-1          BACKGROUND.
UFC 1-200-01, “DoD Building Code” adopts and modifies \3\ International Building Code
2024 (IBC 2024) as the building code for DoD. This UFC adopts the IBC 2024 as the
basis for use in geotechnical engineering design requirements. Chapter 2 of this UFC
further modifies the IBC for specific geotechnical engineering design requirements and
is organized by the IBC chapter that each section modifies.
The required IBC 2024 section modifications are one of four actions, according to the
following legend:
      [Addition] – New section added, includes new section number not shown in IBC
      2024.
      [Deletion] – Delete referenced IBC 2024 section.
      [Replacement] – Delete referenced IBC 2024 section or noted portion and
      replace it with the narrative shown.
      [Supplement] – Add narrative shown as a supplement to the narrative shown in
      the referenced section of IBC 2024. /3/
Effort has been made to adopt non-government standards to the greatest practical
extent when they appear to cover the topics and/or the information contained in the
former manuals, or when they provide new and innovative methods for geotechnical
engineering practices. When non-government criteria does not exist or there is
insufficient coverage of the topic in the non-government criteria and where there are
unique Department of Defense (DoD) requirements, the existing government criteria
from DoD publications are either referenced or have been inserted totally in the
document.
1-2          PURPOSE AND SCOPE.
This Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) provides technical guidance and minimum
technical requirements for geotechnical engineering and design of DoD facilities
worldwide for all service elements. This guidance and the technical requirements are
based on the IBC \3\ 2024 /3/ and the requirements in UFC 1-200-01. This UFC shall
be used by geotechnical engineers to develop military construction contract documents
for design and construction of DoD facilities. Project conditions may dictate the need for
designs that exceed these requirements. This document shall not supersede higher
level mandates such as Public Laws (PL), Executive Orders (E.O.), Regulations (CFR),
DoD Directives (DoDD) and DoD Instructions (DoDI) unless a specific exemption has
been obtained. If a condition or application occurs for which guidance is not provided,
the registered design professional shall obtain guidance from the building official at the
earliest stage of design and prior to commission of any act not easily revised without
cost to the Government.

1-4           APPLICABILITY.
\3\ This UFC follows the same applicability as UFC 1-200-01, paragraph 1-3, with no
exceptions. /3/
1-5          GENERAL BUILDING REQUIREMENTS.
UFC 1-200-01, "DoD Building Code," provides applicability of model building codes and
government-unique criteria for typical design disciplines and building systems, as well
as for accessibility, antiterrorism, security, sustainability, and safety. Use this UFC in
addition to UFC 1-200-01 and the UFCs and government criteria referenced therein. In
addition, comply with all contract documents specific requirements.
1-6          REFERENCES.
Appendix A contains a list of references used in this document. The publication date of
the code or standard is not included in this document. In general, the latest available
issuance of the reference is to be used.
1-7          BEST PRACTICES.
Appendix B identifies background information and practices considered by the DoD as
being acceptable for accomplishing certain geotechnical design and engineering
services. The Engineer of Record (EoR) or Designer of Record (DoR) is expected to
review and interpret this guidance as it conforms to criteria and contract requirements
and apply the information according to the needs of the project. If a Best Practices
document has guidelines or requirements that differ from the UFGS or Unified Facilities
Criteria, the UFGS and the UFC shall prevail.
1-8          SUPPLEMENTAL RESOURCES.
Appendix C provides a list of reliable sources for information on subjects related to
geotechnical engineering, design and construction. These resources are valuable tools
to the geotechnical engineer for additional information on topics pertinent to and
affiliated with geotechnical engineering.
The glossary in Appendix D contains acronyms, abbreviations, and definitions for terms
used in this document.

Settlement constraints govern the design of many shallow foundations and should be
carefully considered prior to a comprehensive consideration of bearing capacity.
Chapter 5 of DM 7.1 provides detailed instructions for settlement calculations. Some

Some structures have widely varying column or wall loads that have the potential to
cause problematic differential settlement. In this case, qall,net can be varied in attempt to
equalize settlements. Often this requires using a lower bearing pressure and larger
footings to support the heavier column loads. If the settlement prone soils are shallow,
it may also be possible to increase the qall,net for the heavily loaded footings by
excavating poor soils and replacing with high-quality compacted structural fill along an
interior line of columns.
At some sites, the depth to rock varies widely and both rock and soil may be found at
the bearing elevation. In this case, differential settlements will be a concern, because of
the dissimilar settlement characteristics of soil and rock. The choice of an appropriate
solution will be informed by both the extent of the dissimiliar bearing condition and the
relative flexibility of the supported structure. One procedure that may be used to reduce

backfill with compacted structural fill. The compacted structural fill should be designed

maximum dry density. A thickness of one to two feet of this type of material will usually
improve the differential settlement characteristics. The length of the transition zone
required to mitigate differential settlement will depend on the flexibility of the structure.
Section 5-6.1 further describes procedures for shallow foundations on fill.
Alternatively, a deepened footing can be reinforced as a grade beam that can allow the
differential settlement to be distributed over a longer span. In other cases, it may be
most economical to use shallow foundations bearing on rock for most of the structure
along with deep foundations and grade beams at the locations where the rock is
deeper.

meet the settlement criteria. As the size of isolated foundations becomes large, the use
of a mat foundation should be considered (see Section 5-4).
Other alternatives to individual shallow foundations are available. If stronger or less
compressible soils are present, the foundation depth may be increased to reach suitable
bearing soils. Another alternative is to excavate and replace unsuitable soils with
compacted structural fill for individual column footings, or in strips along column lines.
Turned down edge foundations integral with the floor slab may be used for lightly loaded
structures. Many of the site improvement techniques discussed in Chapter 1 are
suitable to improve bearing capacity and reduce settlement for shallow foundations.
Some of these techniques work by transferring load to a suitable bearing stratum while
others densify the soil, reducing settlement potential. Useful techniques for shallow
foundations include rigid inclusion piers, aggregate piers, vibro-compaction, dynamic

4.1.2.3 Spacing and Diameter

Stone column diameters vary between 1.5 and 4 feet, but are typically in the range of 3.0 to
3.6 feet for the dry method, and somewhat larger for the wet method.

Triangular, square, or rectangular grid patterns are used, generally with center-to-center
column spacing of 5 to 12 feet. For footing support, they are installed in rows or clusters. For
both footing and wide area support, they should extend beyond the loaded area.

4.1.2.4 Stress Ratio

The relative stiffness of the stone column to the in situ soil, as well as the diameter and
spacing of the columns, determines the sharing of the imposed area vertical load between the
column and the in situ soil.

Since the deflection in the two materials is approximately the same, equilibrium
considerations indicate the stress in the stiffer stone column must be greater than the stress in
the surrounding soil. The assumption of equal deflection is frequently referred to as an equal
strain assumption, which both field measurements and finite element analyses have indicated
to be valid.

The stress concentration or stress ratio n, defined as the stress in stone column divided by the
in situ soil stress, is dependent upon a number of variables, including the relative stiffness
between the two materials, length of the stone column, area ratio and the characteristics of
the granular blanket placed over the stone column. Measured values of stress ratio have
generally been found to be between 2.0 and 5.0, and theory indicates this concentration factor
should increase with time. Since secondary settlement in reinforced cohesive soils is greater
than in the stone column, the long-term stress in the stone column could be larger than at the
end of primary settlement.

column design; and, unfortunately, it is based largely on experience, although theoretical

spacing very tight. For stronger in situ soils and large column spacings, lower bound stress

determined after evaluating settlement of the unimproved soil. A minimum replacement ratio
of 0.33 is generally recommended, as noted in the HITEC Evaluation Report (Collin 2007).

4.2.2   Design Procedures

Rammed aggregate piers are typically selected to increase bearing resistance, reduce
settlement, increase shear strength, or provide any combination of the above.

Preliminary design methods and assumptions to achieve the desired end result are outlined in
this section.

The generalized design process for an embankment support is as follows:

   1. Perform embankment design without rammed aggregate piers to determine the overall
      settlement and global stability to determine if rammed aggregate piers or another
      form of ground improvement are required. If so proceed to step 2.
   2. Assume an area replacement ratio and column diameter.
   3. Determine the spacing based on the assumed area replacement ratio and column
      diameter.
   4. Check the load bearing resistance of the rammed aggregate pier to see if it meets the
      project requirements. If not revise the column diameter and re-check.
   5. Determine the total settlement of the embankment supported on rammed aggregate
      piers.

       changing the column spacing.
    7. Check global stability.
The design process for rammed aggregate piers is similar in many respects to stone columns.
However, the major difference in design of the two systems is with respect to settlement
analysis that is presented in the following sections.

4.2.3     Settlement Analysis

Rammed aggregate pier settlement control design methodology is based on a two-layer
settlement approach as described by Lawton et al. (1994), Fox and Cowell (1998), and
Wissmann et al. (2002). The installation of rammed aggregate piers within the aggregate
column-reinforced zone, referred to as the upper zone, creates a stiffened, engineered zone
with reduced compressibility that reduces settlement of embankments and transportation-
related structures. The settlement below the rammed aggregate pier-reinforced zone, referred
to as the lower-zone, is evaluated using conventional geotechnical analysis approaches. The
total settlement (stot) of the transportation structures is evaluated as the sum of the upper zone
settlement (suz) and the lower zone settlement (slz):

stot = suz + slz                                                                       [Eq. 5-11]

In addition, the stress concentration ratio is related to the stiffness of the matrix soil with
larger ratios resulting at softer soil sites. Suggested stress concentration ratios ranging from 5

A-2               SOILS AND FOUNDATIONS.

A-2.1             Gable Bent Footings.

Moment frame reactions from metal building gable bents have horizontal thrusts at
column bases which can be resisted by several methods. For large thrust forces (40 to
50 kips (118 kN to 222 kN)), tie rods are usually cost-effective. The tie rods can be
embedded in a thickened slab or can be part of a tie beam between column
foundations. For smaller thrust forces, hairpin reinforcing bars may be used to transfer
the thrust force from the column anchor bolts into the slab-on-ground reinforcement,
which acts as the tie between the columns. However, each of these methods requires
close attention to detailing of joints in the slab, isolation joints around a foundation pier
and other possible interruptions in the continuous slab reinforcement between columns.
Also, future renovations that might require trenching across the continuous slab
reinforcement could result in the loss of the tension tie. A third method must design the
foundation for an overturning moment due to the thrust force at the base of the column.
Each of these methods can provide the necessary resistance to the thrust force but
needs to be evaluated for each project condition. For further discussion on the design
of foundations for gable bent reactions, refer to Metal Building Systems: Design and
Specification by Alexander Newman.

A-2.2             Footings on Expansive Soils.

In the presence of expansive soils, footings must be designed to withstand expansive
soil movement in order to prevent significant damage to structures. Cyclical expansive
soil movement from soil water content, usually caused by a combination of inadequate
drainage and seasonal wetting and drying cycles, are especially troublesome. Base the
design on soil testing and recommendations by qualified geotechnical engineers.
Ensure soil investigations include estimates of settlement, heave, and
recommendations to mitigate effects of expansive soil movement. Ensure positive
drainage away from structures that will prevent ponding close to structures. Guidance
on design of foundations on expansive soils can be found in UFC 3-220-01 and PTI DC
10.5-21.

      5.1. Shear Strength. The shear strength Vn provided by concrete (Vc) and reinforcement(Vs)
shall be computed in accordance with ACI 318 except in the cases described in Paragraphs 5.2 to
5.4. Guidance is provided in EM 1110-2-2400 (for outlet works) and EM 1110-2-6053 (for

deep beam provisions of ACI 318.

      5.2. Shear Strength for Cantilevered Walls.

      5.2.1. For cantilever walls, such as in T and L-Type walls, the factored shear in the wall
and footing shall be less than fVc unless shear reinforcement is provided. Shear reinforcement is
not commonly used in walls and wall elements should be designed to eliminate the need for
shear reinforcement.

      5.2.2. The critical section for shear depends on the support conditions. When a
construction joint is used at the base of the stem, the critical section for shear shall be taken at the
base of the stem. Additionally, vertical reinforcement in both faces of the stem should be
developed into the footing to ensure shear friction across the joint. The critical section for shear
in the footing shall be taken at a distance, d, from the front face of the wall stem for the toe
section and at the back face of the wall stem for the heel section. Figure 5-1 shows the critical

   •   Failure in shear along the grout/tendon interface, and

diameter at the surface of rock is projected to the ground surface as a cylinder. The

overlap since the volume of the individual cone will be less. This lowers the allowable

presence of existing underground structures. If the anchor spacing is flexible, the
spacing can be set as 2R, which causes the cones to touch but not overlap.
